tip: A market takes 'op', not 'in': 'op de markt' = at the market.
'Naar' drops the article before places like this: 'naar school', 'naar huis'.
An adverb like 'zorgvuldig' (carefully) usually comes after a definite object: 'onderzoekt de patiënt zorgvuldig'.
A 'het'-word takes no '-e' after 'een': 'een klein dorp', but 'een kleine tuin' for 'de'-words.
Use 'geen' to negate a noun with no article: 'geen broers of zussen' (no brothers or sisters); everything else uses 'niet'.
Jobs take no article after 'zijn': 'ik ben verpleegkundige' (I am a nurse).
Here 'voelen' needs 'me': 'ik voel me' is literally I feel myself, so don't drop the 'me'.
'Kennen' is to know a person or place: 'ken je mijn vriend al?' Facts use 'weten' instead.
Many workplaces take 'op' with no article: 'op kantoor', 'op school'.
'Kijken' needs 'naar' to mean watch: 'ik kijk elke avond naar het journaal'.
Dutch makes homework rather than doing it: 'huiswerk maken', as in 'zij maakt haar huiswerk'.
'Tien over half vier' = 3:40 – ten past the half-hour mark before four.
Separable verbs put 'ge-' in the middle of the past form: 'opgroeien' becomes 'opgegroeid'.
'Trek hebben in' means to fancy or crave: 'ik heb trek in een warme chocolademelk'.
Nouns ending in a single vowel normally add apostrophe-s in the plural: 'pinda's', 'auto's', 'foto's'.
Add 'graag' to soften a wish: 'ik wil graag' means I would like, politer than 'ik wil'.
'Niet' usually follows the verb it negates: 'de auto start niet' (the car does not start).
'Schrijven aan' is to write to: 'een brief aan haar moeder'. The recipient takes 'aan'.
Nationalities are capitalized nouns and normally take no article: 'ik ben Nederlander'.
Wellbeing uses 'gaan' plus 'met': 'het goed met je gaat' is literally it goes well with you (you are doing well).
'Op zoek naar' is a fixed phrase for looking for: 'ik ben op zoek naar een nieuw appartement'.
With 'sinds', Dutch stays in the present: 'ik heb pijn in mijn rug sinds gisteren' means I have had back pain since yesterday.
You follow a course in Dutch: 'een cursus volgen' means to take a course.
The prefix 'schoon-' turns a family word into the in-law version: 'schoonmoeder' (mother-in-law), 'schoonvader', 'schoonzus'.
'Ons' means both our and us: 'voor ons' means for us.
'Lachen om' is to laugh at: 'zij lacht altijd om zijn grappen', with 'om' where English uses at.
Use 'elk' before 'het'-words and 'elke' before 'de'-words: 'elk station' ('het'), 'elke dag' ('de').
'Lenen' means both to borrow and to lend; here 'hij leent boeken bij de bibliotheek' means he borrows books from the library.
'Bank' means both couch and bank; context decides: here 'op de bank' is on the couch.
Clock times take 'om': 'om acht uur' means at eight o'clock.
